title: Topic 7 Changing towns and cities - Hodder practice questions

questions.question_text: Figure 7.23 shows changes in urban and rural populations by region between 1950 and 2050 (predicted from 2025). State the continent with the largest number of urban dwellers in 2025.

points: Asia (accept North America if referring to percentage urbanisation) [1]
marking_scheme.rubric: Award 1 mark for Asia (or North America according to textbook mark scheme note).

questions.question_text: State the decade when 50 per cent of the population in Latin America and the Caribbean lived in urban areas.
Describe the trend in levels of urbanisation in Europe between 1950 and 2050 (predicted from 2025).

points: Levels of urbanisation increased rapidly between 1950 and 1980 [1], rising from just over 50% to about 70% [1]
Growth slowed down after 1980, reaching approximately 75% by 2025 [1]
Predicted to increase steadily to about 80% by 2050 [1]
marking_scheme.rubric: Award up to 3 marks for describing the rapid early phase, slowing middle phase, and projected future with data.

questions.question_text: Figure 7.24 shows seasonal variations in air quality in Delhi. Explain the seasonal variations in air quality in Delhi.

points: Air quality in Delhi varies between borderline satisfactory and very poor / severe [1]
Borderline satisfactory air quality during the monsoon rainy season (July to September) because heavy rainfall washes pollutants out of the air [1]
Air quality deteriorates rapidly and reaches hazardous/severe levels between October and January due to Diwali fireworks and stubble burning of paddy residue [1]
Another spike occurs in April and May caused by regional dust storms and wheat stubble burning [1]
Year-round baseline pollution is sustained by thermal power plants, vehicle exhaust, brick kilns, and diesel generators [1]
marking_scheme.rubric: Award up to 5 marks for explaining monsoon cleansing, autumn peak (Diwali/paddy), spring peak (dust/wheat), and background urban emissions.

questions.question_text: Figure 7.25 shows a development on the rural-to-urban fringe. Define the term 'rural-to-urban fringe'.

points: The zone / transition area where the urban sprawl / built-up edge of a town meets the surrounding rural countryside [1]
marking_scheme.rubric: Award 1 mark for defining rural-to-urban fringe as the boundary zone where city meets countryside.

questions.question_text: Suggest the advantages of the rural-to-urban fringe for new developments.

points: Cheaper land prices compared to congested Central Business Districts (CBD) [1]
Abundance of open space / greenfield land allowing large horizontal layouts (business parks, shopping malls, housing estates) and ample parking [1]
Excellent transport connectivity with motorway junctions, bypasses, ring roads, and airports [1]
Pleasant, cleaner environment with less noise and air pollution [1]
marking_scheme.rubric: Award up to 3 marks for suggesting three distinct commercial, transport, or environmental advantages.

questions.question_text: Assess the likely impacts of new developments in the rural-to-urban fringe on the environment.

points: Negative impacts: Loss of agricultural farmland and natural habitats / greenfield sites; deforestation and fragmentation of ecosystems [1]
Increased air, noise, and light pollution from rising commuter traffic [1]
Higher surface runoff and flooding risk due to impermeable concrete surfaces (roads, roofs, parking lots) replacing soil [1]
Positive / mitigated impacts: Creation of landscaped green buffers, wildlife ponds, and sustainable drainage systems (SuDS) in modern developments [1]
marking_scheme.rubric: Award up to 4 marks for assessing negative environmental impacts with potential mitigations.

questions.question_text: For a named example, assess the challenges and opportunities of urban living.

inputs.label: Nhập bài làm Case Study (7 marks):

points: Named example: e.g. London, Mumbai, Rio de Janeiro, Shanghai, or Cairo [1 mark]

Opportunities: Employment diversity and higher wages in formal sector; superior educational institutions and healthcare; cultural attractions, entertainment, and modern infrastructure; social mobility [2-3 marks]

Challenges: Severe traffic congestion and air pollution; squatter settlements / shanty towns (e.g. Dharavi in Mumbai, Favelas in Rio) with lack of clean water/sanitation; high crime rates; housing unaffordability and social inequality [2-3 marks]
Assessment / Evaluation: Weighing whether city management and economic benefits outweigh the environmental and social drawbacks [1 mark]
marking_scheme.rubric: Level 1 (1-3 marks): General statements about urban life without named example or balance. Level 2 (4-6 marks): Detailed explanation of both opportunities and challenges for a named city. Level 3 (7 marks): Balanced and sophisticated assessment evaluating opportunities vs challenges for a specific named city, concluding with an evaluative judgement.
